cases.title: The first shape
cases.needle: Then I hit a wall, and it is the wall this whole document is about.
cases.before_tex: Then I hit a wall, and it is the wall this whole document is about. Z3 could settle the small questions and fell over on the exact ones I needed answered, which left me staring down an infinite hallway of guess-and-test with no proof waiting at the end of it, ever. One night, not even working, I was watching a video about Flatland, the old story about a creature living in two dimensions who cannot so much as picture a third. And it landed on me sideways, all at once, the way the real ones always do. I said it out loud: I get it now. There is another axis. Classical computation only ever sees what it can read and write off its own surface, and there is a whole direction it is blind to. It isn't broken. It was just never built with an eye that points that way. The two computers on the first pages of this book are my attempt to show you that blindness with something you can hold. I opened a new repo that same night and called the thing in it the Thiele Machine. The name began as a working title and became the name of the model. It carries the larger claim plainly: the machine treats structural state as part of computation.

cases.title: What the record does
cases.before_tex:
It isn't more computing power. Anything a Thiele machine computes, the
machine under its record
computes without it. The book proves that over any machine at all, a base-driven record is a switch the machine's own
events flip once and nothing flips back; it watches the computing and adds nothing to it. It isn't
faster. It isn't quantum. It says nothing about which problems are hard.
cases.after_tex:
It isn't more computing power. Anything a Thiele machine computes, the
machine under its record
computes without it. The book proves that over any machine at all, a base-driven record is a switch the machine's own
events flip once and nothing flips back; it watches the computing and adds nothing to it. That's
a sentence about the record. The checker belongs to the machine under it, and the definition of
Thiele-complete doesn't ask the checker to be a program. Hand it a checker that knows which
programs halt, and whether a CHECK of ``this program halts'' traps tells you whether it does, so
that machine decides halting (Section~\ref{sec:smallest} has the details). With a checker that is a program, as
every checker in this book is, nothing in the machine goes past what a program can do. The record
makes nothing faster either: erase the flag and the counter, and every run takes the same steps to
the same places. CHECK is another matter. It's a test at unit cost, and one CHECK of ``$A \ge m$''
settles whether $A \ge m$ in one step, where the two counters alone would count $A$ down. It isn't
quantum. It says nothing about which problems are hard.

cases.title: What a program cannot do
cases.needle: The second says that even if reading were free,
cases.before_tex: The second says that even if reading were free, a fixed program couldn't. It's the pigeonhole.
cases.after_tex:
The second says that even if reading were free, a fixed program couldn't keep them by sending each
guest property to one of a fixed, finite list of host properties and checking it on the same
register the guest's fact is about. That's all the theorem below rules out, and it's the
pigeonhole.

cases.title: What deserves a record
cases.needle: Of all the events a machine could put on its meter,
cases.before_tex:
Of all the events a machine could put on its meter, the ones its price list charges for and
its counter adds up, certification is the one whose records
get \emph{copied}: checked, stored, and relied on across independent places that share no other
state. Rival events leave no such trail. If that's true, the choice of certification stops being free.
It's the one event the world around the machine keeps redundant copies of, and that's a
reason to price it and leave the others unpriced.
cases.after_tex:
Of all the events a machine could put on its meter, the ones its price list charges for and
its counter adds up, certification is the one whose records
get \emph{copied and relied on by parties who didn't produce them}: checked, stored, and acted on
across independent places that share no other state. Copying alone can't be the test. A
replicated system copies everything it holds to every node, the gas used in a block header as
faithfully as the word final, so rival events get copied too. Nobody who didn't produce them
acts on them. If that's true, the choice of certification stops being free.
It's the one event the world around the machine keeps redundant copies of and leans on, and that's a
reason to price it and leave the others unpriced. So the thesis has two halves, and the ways to
kill it at the end aim at both: certification is that event, and where a deployed discipline puts
a price on writing a record, the record it prices is one that's copied and relied on in that sense.
